opts: Bacterial invasion of all bowel-wall layers

questions.q: Which condition is included among the IBS associations?
questions.exp: The association list includes lactose intolerance, celiac disease, fibromyalgia, chronic fatigue syndrome and generalized anxiety disorder. (Book p63)

questions.q: Which pair is also listed as IBS-associated on p63?
questions.exp: Celiac disease and fibromyalgia are both in the associations list. (Book p63)

questions.q: Which neuropsychiatric/functional pair appears in the IBS associations list?
opts: Chronic fatigue syndrome and generalized anxiety disorder
questions.exp: The page lists chronic fatigue syndrome and generalized anxiety disorder. (Book p63)

questions.exp: The clinical-presentation section states female > male. (Book p63)

questions.sec: Clinical Pattern, Rome IV and Red Flags
questions.q: The age group specified in the IBS clinical-presentation list is:
questions.exp: The page gives age <45 years. (Book p63)

questions.sec: Clinical Pattern, Rome IV and Red Flags
questions.q: Which symptom is marked as the most important in the IBS presentation?
questions.exp: Abdominal pain is marked as the most important symptom. (Book p63)

questions.sec: Clinical Pattern, Rome IV and Red Flags
questions.q: The page's Rome IV line requires recurrent abdominal pain at least how often?
questions.exp: The book prints a minimum of one episode/week for ≥3 months. It omits Rome IV’s symptom-onset ≥6-month criterion; see audit/known-source-caveats.md. (Book p63)

questions.sec: Clinical Pattern, Rome IV and Red Flags
questions.q: For how long does the p63 Rome IV line require the weekly pain pattern?
questions.exp: The page states ≥3 months. (Book p63)

questions.q: The Rome IV line requires the pain to be associated with at least how many of the listed stool/defecation features?
questions.exp: The page says pain is associated with ≥2 of the listed features. (Book p63)

questions.q: Which group contains the three associated features shown in the Rome IV line?
opts: Change in stool frequency; change in stool form; relation to defecation
Fever; blood in stool; raised ESR
questions.exp: The three printed features are change in stool frequency, change in stool form/appearance and relation to defecation. (Book p63)

questions.sec: Clinical Pattern, Rome IV and Red Flags
questions.q: The typical pain location is described as:
questions.exp: The page describes crampy lower-abdominal pain. (Book p63)

questions.sec: Clinical Pattern, Rome IV and Red Flags
questions.q: The pain frequency listed in the clinical section is:
opts: Only after meals, several times per hour
questions.exp: The source notes episodic pain at approximately one episode per week. (Book p63)

questions.sec: Clinical Pattern, Rome IV and Red Flags
questions.q: Which pair of factors is listed as aggravating IBS pain?
questions.exp: Stress and eating are listed as aggravating factors. (Book p63)

questions.sec: Clinical Pattern, Rome IV and Red Flags

questions.exp: Defecation is listed as a relieving factor. (Book p63)

questions.sec: Clinical Pattern, Rome IV and Red Flags
questions.q: Which symptom is called the most consistent in the IBS presentation?
questions.exp: Altered bowel habits are marked as the most consistent symptom. (Book p63)

questions.sec: Clinical Pattern, Rome IV and Red Flags
questions.q: In the D+ pattern, diarrhoea is described as:
questions.exp: D+ is diarrhoea-predominant with small-volume stool associated with mucus. (Book p63)

questions.q: Which label is used for constipation-predominant IBS?
questions.exp: The page labels constipation-predominant disease C+. (Book p63)

questions.exp: M+ is marked m/c and described as prolonged constipation interrupted by episodic diarrhoea. (Book p63)

questions.sec: Clinical Pattern, Rome IV and Red Flags
questions.q: A patient with suspected IBS reports nocturnal diarrhoea and visible blood in stool. These findings are listed as:

opts: Crampy lower-abdominal pain relieved by defecation
Steatorrhoea, weight loss, anaemia or malabsorption
Mucus with small-volume D+ stool alone
questions.exp: Steatorrhoea, weight loss, anaemia and malabsorption are listed as features against IBS. (Book p63)

questions.sec: Clinical Pattern, Rome IV and Red Flags
questions.q: Which systemic finding is included among features against an IBS diagnosis?
questions.exp: Fever is included among features against IBS. (Book p63)

questions.exp: The warning list includes increased ESR. (Book p63)

questions.exp: The clinical list includes abdominal distension and belching. (Book p63)

questions.q: Which upper-GI symptom is listed under IBS clinical presentations?
questions.exp: Dyspepsia/heartburn is listed. (Book p63)

questions.sec: Clinical Pattern, Rome IV and Red Flags
questions.q: The remaining paired symptoms in the p63 presentation list are:

questions.exp: The first listed theory is visceral hypersensitivity. (Book p64)

questions.q: In the visceral-hypersensitivity model, minimal rectal distension can:
opts: Suppress pain receptors until very high volume
Stimulate pain receptors because sensitivity is enhanced
questions.exp: The page says minimal rectal distension stimulates pain receptors due to enhanced sensitivity. (Book p64)

questions.q: Compared with healthy controls, the graph demonstrates rectal hypersensitivity in IBS because pain/sensation occurs at:
opts: The same volume in every subject
questions.exp: The IBS curve rises at lower distending volumes than the healthy-control curve. (Book p64)

questions.q: Which additional motor abnormality appears second in the p64 pathophysiology list?
questions.exp: The second listed mechanism is increased colonic motor potentials. (Book p64)

questions.q: The central nervous system structure named in the IBS list is the:
questions.exp: The page lists central activation of the cingulate cortex. (Book p64)

questions.exp: The page lists an increase in serotonin-containing enterochromaffin cells. (Book p64)

questions.q: Which ion-channel family is the fifth item in the pathophysiology list?
questions.exp: The final listed pathophysiology item is vanilloid channels (TRP-V1). (Book p64)

questions.q: The p64 lifestyle flowchart estimates improvement after diet and lifestyle modifications in:
questions.exp: The flowchart gives improvement in 70% of cases. (Book p64)

Fermentable oligo-, di-, monosaccharides and polyols

questions.exp: Examples listed include apple, mango, wheat, honey, legumes and cauliflower. (Book p64)

opts: Bloating, distension, flatulence, abdominal pain and constipation

opts: True — but only for C+ IBS
True — the note says effectiveness is not determined

False — the note addresses only loperamide
questions.exp: The final note says effectiveness of antibiotics, probiotics and prebiotics is not determined. (Book p65)

units.title: Definition & Associations
units.guide:
IBS is presented as a functional bowel disorder/reaction to stress.
Associations: lactose intolerance, celiac disease, fibromyalgia, chronic fatigue and generalized anxiety.
The clinical list is more common in women and under age 45.

units.title: Clinical Pattern, Rome IV & Red Flags
units.sec: Clinical Pattern, Rome IV and Red Flags
units.guide:
Pain: crampy lower abdomen, at least weekly, aggravated by stress/eating and relieved by defecation.
Rome IV line as printed: ≥3 months and ≥2 of stool-frequency change, stool-form change or defecation relation; the source omits onset ≥6 months before diagnosis (see audit/known-source-caveats.md).
Nocturnal diarrhoea, blood, fever, weight loss, anaemia, malabsorption and raised ESR argue against IBS.

units.title: Pathophysiology
units.guide:
Visceral hypersensitivity, increased colonic motor potentials and cingulate activation are listed.
The page also notes serotonin-containing enterochromaffin cells and TRP-V1 channels.
The graph shows pain/sensation at lower rectal distending volumes in IBS.

units.title: Lifestyle & FODMAPs
units.guide:
Diet/lifestyle changes improve about 70%; walking target is 6,000–8,000 steps.
Reduce fermentable oligo-, di-, monosaccharides and polyols; examples include apple, mango, wheat, honey, legumes and cauliflower.
Water draw in small bowel and fermentation/gas in colon explain the diagrammed symptoms.

units.title: Type-Based Medical Management
units.guide:
D+: loperamide, pre-meal antispasmodic, antidepressant; the table labels several drugs obsolete.
C+: psyllium/PEG, lubiprostone, linaclotide and tenapanor.
Keep each table drug linked to its action/adverse effect; the source says antibiotic/probiotic/prebiotic effectiveness is undetermined.
